Breathing-mode oscillations in Hall thrusters

Ada Physicist, David J. Bohm, Irving Langmuir

Abstract

The breathing mode is a low-frequency oscillation of the discharge current in Hall thrusters. We measure its frequency across operating conditions and relate it to ionization front motion in the channel.

Share Cite this article

1. Introduction

Hall thrusters are electric propulsion devices used for satellite station keeping and orbit raising. Their discharge current oscillates at tens of kilohertz in the so-called breathing mode, first described by predator-prey models of neutral depletion and ionization.

Understanding these oscillations matters because they couple to the power processing unit and can limit stable operation at high power.

2. Method

We operated a 1.5 kW laboratory thruster on xenon at discharge voltages from 200 to 400 V. The plasma potential was measured with an emissive probe, and the current with a Hall-effect sensor sampled at 10 MHz.

2.1 Probe analysis

The electron temperature follows from the slope of the probe characteristic, with T in electronvolts. Corrections for sheath expansion were applied throughout the analysis of the probe traces.

3. Results

3.2 Frequency scaling

The breathing-mode frequency rose from 14 kHz at 200 V to 23 kHz at 400 V, roughly linearly with the square root of the discharge voltage. This agrees with the predator-prey scaling within ten percent across the full range of operating points.

4. Conclusion

The breathing-mode frequency scales predictably with voltage, which gives a simple design rule for avoiding resonance with the power supply filter in flight hardware.
